If "the Book" means the whole Book, then it indicates that its revelation is like the sending down of the whole in achieving the purpose of challenge and warning. So the claim that this aspect is free of any beneficial point is free of any fair consideration. If the letters are taken as a mere enumeration, then they have no share in i'rab, and ﴿revelation﴾ is the predicate of an implied subject indicated by what precedes it, meaning: "what is composed of the kind mentioned is the revelation of the Book," or it is a subject whose predicate is the adverbial phrase after it, according to what Jar Allah said. It has also been said: ḥā' mīm is a thing sworn by, so there is an implied preposition in it, and it is in a position of genitive or accusative according to the known disagreement about this. And ﴿revelation﴾ is a detached (maqṭū') attribute, so it is the predicate of an implied subject, and the sentence is a new independent sentence, and it is the answer of the oath.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 3:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, in the heavens and the earth are signs for the believers﴾. According to what has preceded, it is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) serving to draw attention to the cosmic signs (al-ayat al-takwiniyyah).

It is also permissible that ﴿The revelation of the Book is from Allah﴾ be a subject and predicate, with the sentence serving as the answer to the oath (jawab al-qasam). This is contrary to the apparent meaning. It has also been said that Ha Mim is taken as the oath-subject (muqsam bihi), a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, meaning "Ha Mim is my oath," and that "revelation" (tanzil) is then a qualifier of it, not separated (ghayr maqtu'). In all the other possibilities, His saying, Glorified is He: ﴿the Almighty, the All-Wise﴾ is a qualifier of the Divine Name (al-ism al-jalil).

Al-Imam (al-Razi) permitted that it be an attribute of the Book (sifah lil-kitab), but he preferred the first view, since this requires resorting to metaphor (almajaz) and the attribute is closer to the qualified noun in the first view. Abu Hayyan made it obligatory, because the second view involves a separation (fasl) between the attribute and the qualified noun, which is not permissible.

As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, in the heavens...﴾ and so on, it may be that there is an omitted noun by way of elision (taqdir mudaf), meaning: "Indeed, in the creation of the heavens..." as al-Wahidi related from al-Zajjaj, because this has been stated explicitly in another verse, and the Qur'an explains one part of itself by another. This is supported by His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 4:

﴿And in your creation﴾ to its end. It is also permissible that it be taken in its apparent sense, and in that case it is one of two aspects. The first: that in them (the heavens and the earth) are signs, i.e. what is in them of created things, such as the mountains, the minerals, the stars and the two luminaries (the sun and the moon). In this case, His, the Exalted's, words ﴿and in your creation﴾ are an instance of specific (khass) being conjoined to general ('amm) (ʿatf al-khass ʿala al-ʿamm). The second: that the heavens and the earth themselves are signs, because of the various kinds of indication in them of the All-Powerful, the All-Wise, exalted is His majesty. This is the more apparent, and it is more eloquent than saying: "Indeed, in their creation are signs," although the meaning returns to that. ﴿And in your creation﴾ is a preposed predicate (khabar muqaddam), and His, the Exalted's, words ﴿and what He disperses of living creatures﴾ are conjoined to "creation" (khalq). It is permitted that "ma" be a verbal noun (masdariyyah), or a relative pronoun (mawsulah), either with an elided genitive (taqdir mudaf), i.e. "and in the creation of what He spreads and scatters of living creatures," or without it.

It is also permitted that it be conjoined to the attached pronoun in the genitive by annexation, with "ma" being a relative pronoun only, according to the apparent reading. This is based on the permissibility of conjoining to an attached pronoun in the genitive without repeating the preposition, which is the position of the Kufans, Yunus and al-Akhfash. Abu Hayyan said: this is the correct view, and al-Ustadh Abu Ali al-Shalubin chose it. The position of Sibawayh and the majority of the Basrans is the prohibition of the said conjunction, whether the pronoun is genitive by a particle or by annexation, due to the strength of the connection, so it resembles conjunction to part of a word.

Ibn al-Hajib mentioned in his commentary on al-Mufassal, in the chapter on pausing, that some grammarians permit conjunction with a genitive by annexation but not with a genitive by a particle, because the connection of the genitive to the annexed noun is not like its connection to a particle, since each of the two is independent with its own meaning, so its connection is not as strong as with the particle. Al-Jirmi and al-Ziyadi permitted conjunction when the attached pronoun is emphasized by a separate pronoun, as in "I passed by you, you and Zayd" (marartu bika anta wa Zaydin). And His, the Exalted's, words ﴿signs﴾ are a delayed subject (mubtada' mu'akhkhar), and the sentence is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Indeed, in the heavens﴾ etc.

Ubayy and ʿAbdullah read (la-ayatun) with the lam. Thus reported in al-Bahr, but it did not state whether "ayatin" is nominative or accusative. If it is accusative, the lam is an added particle in the noun of "inna" which precedes its predicate, and this is one of the regular, frequent places of its addition. If it is nominative, then it is an added lam in the subject, and its addition there is rare. The beauty of its addition here is the preceding of "inna" in the sentence conjoined to it, so it is like his saying:

"Indeed the caliphate after them is blameworthy, and successors are a stage of what I despise."

Zayd ibn ʿAli read (ayatun) in the singular. Al-Aʿmash, al-Jahdari, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Yaʿqub read (ayatin) in the plural and the accusative, on the basis that it is conjoined to the earlier "ayatin", which is the noun of "inna", since ﴿and in your creation﴾ is conjoined to ﴿in the heavens﴾. It is as if it were said: "Indeed, in your creation and what He disperses of living creatures are signs ﴿for a people who have certainty﴾", i.e. it is among their nature to be certain of things as they are. ﴿And the alternation of night and day﴾ is in the genitive by implied "fi" (in). ʿAbdullah read it with the mention of the preposition. The elision of the genitive particle with retention of its governing has occurred, as in his saying:

"When it is said, 'Which of the people is the worst tribe?', the Kulayb point with the tips of their fingers."

What makes the mention of the particle in the two preceding verses suitable here is that it was mentioned before. It was also read in the nominative, as a subject whose predicate is afterwards "ayatun". What is meant by their alternation is their succession, or their variation in length and shortness. It is also said: their difference is that one of them is light and the other darkness.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 5:**

﴿And what Allah sends down﴾ is in conjunction (ʿaṭf) with (the alternation of) ﴿from the sky﴾, meaning the direction above. It is said: the clouds. It is also said: the celestial body known by a kind of interpretation.

﴿of provision﴾ means of rain. It is called provision because it is its cause, so the usage is metaphorical (majaz). Even without this interpretation it would be correct, since it is in itself a provision too.

﴿and by it gives life to the earth﴾ by bringing forth from it kinds of grain, fruits and plants. The causal link is customary, a pattern required by wisdom.

[Page 140]

﴿after its death﴾ its dryness and barrenness, its being void of the traces of life, and the absence of the power of growth in it. ﴿And the turning of the winds﴾ from one direction to another and from one state to another. Its being placed after the sending down of rain, although it precedes it in existence, is either to indicate that it is an independent sign, since if the existential order had been observed it might have been thought that the combination of the turning of the winds and the sending down of rain is a single sign; or because the turning of the winds being a sign is not merely due to its being the origin of the production of rain, but also to it and to the other benefits, among which is the driving of ships through the seas.

Zayd ibn ʿAli, Talha and ʿIsa read (the turning of the wind) in the singular. ﴿Are signs for a people who understand﴾ with the nominative (marfuʿ) on the basis that it is a subject (mubtadaʾ) whose predicate is what preceded it, namely the prepositional phrase ﴿in the alternation of﴾ as you have heard, and the sentence is in conjunction with what came before it.

It is said that (the alternation of) with the genitive (majrur) is in conjunction with ﴿your creation﴾, which is genitive by the preposition ﴿in﴾ before it, and ﴿signs﴾ is in conjunction with the earlier ﴿signs﴾ which is nominative as a subject. In this there is conjunction on the two objects (maʿmul) of two different governing words (ʿamil). Some people prohibit this, and they are most of the Basran grammarians; some permit it, and they are most of the Kufan grammarians; and some make a distinction, saying: it is permissible in a phrase like "In the house is Zayd and in the room is ʿAmr", but not permissible in a phrase like "Zayd is in the house and ʿAmr the room", because in the first the genitive (majrur) is immediately preceded by the conjunction, so the conjunction stands in place of the preposition, while in the second the genitive is not immediately after the conjunction, so the preposition would have to be omitted without a replacement. The full discussion of this question belongs in its proper place.

It is said that (the alternation of) is in conjunction with the genitive before it, and ﴿signs﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are signs. This is the view chosen by those who do not permit conjunction on two governed words, and who hold that the omission of the preposition while its government remains is weak even when a preposition has been mentioned before.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿signs﴾ is nominative as an emphatic restatement (taʾkid) of the earlier ﴿signs﴾; they repeat a word when the sentence is long, for emphasis and reminder. This has been objected to on the ground that such repetition is only of the very same thing, whereas the difference of the attributes indicates a difference of the things described, so there is no basis for emphasis. Moreover, it involves separating the genitive conjoined word from what it is conjoined to, and the emphatic from what it emphasises; and even if this is permissible, it produces an obscurity that is incompatible with the eloquence of the Great Qur'an.

Whoever reads ﴿signs﴾ here in the accusative, as he reads it there, then it is the object of an omitted verb, meaning: I mean signs. It is said: the conjunction in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and the alternation of﴾, conjoins the alternation to the genitive by the earlier ﴿in﴾, and its conjunction to the noun of ʾinna is based on permissibility of conjunction on two governed words.

Abu al-Baqa' said: ﴿signs﴾ is in the accusative as an emphatic repetition of the noun of ʾinna, as in: "Indeed, on your garment is blood, and on Zayd's garment is blood." What is objectionable in this has been mentioned just above.

Some said: it is the noun of ʾinna, with an omitted ʾinna, and ʾinna may be omitted while its government remains. Abu Hayyan mentioned in al-Irtishaf, in discussing ʾinna in the phrase "Indeed the best of people or the best of them is Zayd", that Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn al-Mubarak al-Yazidi held that "the best of them" is in the accusative and "Zayd" in the nominative; the noun of ʾinna is omitted, and "or the best of them" is accusative by an omitted ʾinna, indicated by the mentioned ʾinna. Its estimated form is: "Indeed, of the best of people, Zayd; and indeed, the best of them is Zayd." Al-Shatibi approved of deriving the accusative in the verse on this basis, but al-Safaqisi transmitted it from Abu al-Baqa' and rejected it on the ground that ʾinna is not omitted.

Ibn Hisham said at the end of the fourth chapter of al-Mughni: it is remote, and the apparent view is that it must be accompanied by omitting the preposition in (the alternation of), and in that case its position is not hidden.

All the other readings are transmitted here from the same people from whom they were transmitted earlier. The indefinite form of ﴿signs﴾ in the verses is for magnification, in quantity and in quality. The meaning is: fair-minded servants, when they look at the heavens and the earth with correct observation, know that they are created and that they must have a Creator, so they believe in Allah, exalted is He, and affirm it. When they look at their own creation, their transitions from state to state and form to form, and at the creation of what is on the surface of the earth of the various kinds of living beings, their faith increases and they become certain, and doubt is removed from them. Then when they look at the other events that renew themselves at every moment, such as the alternation of night and day, the descent of rain, the life of the earth after its death, and the turning of the winds, south and north, the east wind and the west wind, strong and weak, hot and cold, they understand, their knowledge is firmly established and their certainty is pure. So it is in the Kashshaf, and from this the reason for the variation of the closing rhymes (fawasil) becomes known.

In al-Kashf it is mentioned, in summary, that this is by way of ascent (taraqqi), and this agrees with what the Sufis and others hold, that certainty (iqan) is a special rank within faith. Then intellect, since faith and certainty depend on it, by which is meant the intellect strengthened by the light of insight, is made to be (the final element) because certainty is purified from the intrusion of doubts from every direction, so in its firm establishment is all good. The order of the signs follows the order of the three ranks, placing first what is earlier in existence. It does not follow that the second sign must be greater than the first, or the third than the second, because the one who combines the two observations is certain, and the one who combines the three is intelligent; and it is so in attaining this aim. If one of them is greater in some other respect, there is no harm, since looking at one's own self and what is of its kind, then its genus among the other humans and animals, is more effective in removing doubt and attaining certainty because of nearness, repetition and great numbers. And if looking at the heavens and the earth is more complete in indicating the perfection of power and knowledge, that does no harm, and it is not what is sought here. Then looking at the alternation mentioned is more indicative of the firm establishment of that certainty, in that it renews itself from time to time and urges observation and reflection each time it renews. The truth is that the complete observation of the second requires observation of the first, because the heavens and the earth are in some respect causes of the coming into being of living beings. Likewise observation of the third requires observation of the first two. As for the first, that is evident; as for the second, it is because it is the final cause, so it must be comprehensive. End of quotation. This is a very precious statement.

Al-Imam (al-Razi) said regarding the order of these closing rhymes: I think the reason is that it was said: if you are believers, understand these proofs; and if you are not believers but are seekers of conviction and certainty, understand these proofs; and if you are neither believers nor certain, then you must at least be among the company of the intelligent. So strive to know these proofs. It is not hidden that he missed this verification and did not choose the ascending order, though it is truly right to choose it. The difference between what is here and what is in Surat al-Baqara, namely ﴿Indeed, in the creation of the heavens and the earth, and the alternation of night and day, and the ships that run in the sea with what benefits people...﴾ up to the end of the verse, is for variety of expression, and eloquent speech is full of this. Al-Imam mentioned in this matter what does not stir the listener, so reflect carefully.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 6:**

﴿Those are the signs of God﴾ is a mubtada' (subject) and khabar (predicate). His statement, exalted is He, ﴿We recite them to you﴾ is a hal (circumstantial clause), its 'amil (governing element) being the meaning of the demonstrative (ma'na al-ishara), as in ﴿and this is my husband, an old man﴾, according to the well-known view. It was also said that the khabar is ﴿We recite them to you﴾ and that ﴿the signs of God﴾ is a badal (substitute) or 'atf bayan (explicative apposition). His statement, glorified is He, ﴿in truth﴾ is a hal from the subject of ﴿We recite them﴾ or from its object, meaning: We recite them while being truthful, or while being associated with truth. The ba' is then for mulabasa (association). It is also permissible for it to be for sababiyya (causation) or ghayiyya (indicating the end purpose).

The signs referred to may be the signs of the Qur'an, or the surah, or what was mentioned earlier of the heavens, the earth and other things. So their recitation is by the recitation of what indicates them. It has also been interpreted as sard (continuous narration), i.e., We narrate them to you.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the speech is with an omitted mudaf (possessive noun), i.e., We recite their matter and the matter of the lesson in them. It was read as ﴿yatluwha﴾ with the ya' (third person), so that the agent is His pronoun, exalted is He. According to both readings, the intended meaning is their recitation to him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, through the mediation of the angel, peace be upon him.

﴿Then in what statement after God and His signs will they believe?﴾ This is of the type of their saying: "Zayd has impressed me and his generosity," meaning "The generosity of Zayd has impressed me," except that they deviated from it for the sake of emphasis in the admiration. The meaning is: then in what statement after these recited signs, which are in truth, will they believe? In this there is an indication that there is no clearer explanation than this explanation, and no sign more indicative than this sign. The glorification of the status of the signs comes from the demonstrative, from their attribution to God, mighty and majestic is He, from making ﴿We recite them﴾ a hal together with the pronoun of exaltation, then from repeating the sublime Name for the stated purpose, and from attributing them to Him through a pronoun a second time. Al-Zamakhshari mentioned this, and Abu Hayyan criticized it, saying that it is worthless, because in it there is, in terms of meaning, the insertion of nouns without necessity and the 'atf (conjunction). What is meant is other than 'atf, namely removing it to the category of badal, because the estimate "generosity of Zayd" only occurs in "a'jabani Zayd kараmuhu" (Zayd impressed me, his generosity) without a waw, as a badal. This is an inversion of the realities of grammar. The meaning in the example is only that the essence of Zayd impressed him and his generosity impressed him, so there are two admirations, not one admiration. This is based on not probing deeply into the understanding of the speech of Jar Allah (the Divine Neighbour, i.e., al-Zamakhshari).

Whoever probes deeply into it does not see that he (al-Zamakhshari) holds the view of insertion; rather, it is an explanation of the resulting meaning which gives that impression. Between this method and the method of badal there is complete difference. It has been mentioned that the benefit of this method, which is the method of attributing the verb to one thing while the intended attribution is to what is conjoined to it, is the strength of the specialness of the conjoined thing with the thing it is conjoined to, from the perspective of indicating that it has reached such a degree of association that it is valid to attribute its qualities, actions and states to the first intentionally, because it is in its position. This is not so with badal, because the intention in it, relative to the matter, is only the second. Here both are intended. If you say: if that quality is not attributed to the thing conjoined to, it entails insertion, as Abu Hayyan said, and what is mentioned of exaggeration does not remove the problem; and even if it is granted, its indication of what was mentioned is by which of the well-known modes of indication?

It was answered: it is not attributed to it in reality, but since there is a complete association between them from some aspect, such as the signs here being by His permission, or being pleasing to Him, mighty and majestic is He, it is treated as if it were the intended attribution, and that specialness is expressed by it as an indirect allusive metonymy (kinaya ima'iyya). Then the attributed thing is conjoined to it and made a follower in it. With this it differs from badal with complete difference, which the objector overlooked. So the attribution in its entirety is metaphorical. This is how some of the verifiers (muhaqqiqin) established it.

Al-Wahidi said: meaning, then in what statement after the statement of God, i.e., the Qur'an. Its application to it has come in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿God has sent down the best statement﴾. The pronominal reference is good because of the indicator of the prior mention of "statement". His statement, glorified is He, ﴿and His signs﴾ is conjoined to it, because they differ in general and specific terms, for the signs are that statement viewed in its parts. If what is intended is what is clarified in it of signs and proofs, then it is not 'atf al-khass 'ala al-'amm (conjoining the specific to the general), because the signs are not part of the Qur'an; rather, the aspect of their indication and their inclusion in it is what is meant. In this aspect there is also an indication of the state of explanation and what is explained, as in the first aspect.

Al-Dahhak said: meaning, then in what statement after the tawhid of God. It is clear that in its apparent sense this has no meaning, so perhaps he intended "after the statement of His tawhid", i.e., the statement containing that; or it is "after" with an estimated mudaf, from the type of "a'jabani Zayd wa karamuhu". Whichever it is, the fa' is in the answer of an estimated conditional, and the adverbial phrase is an attribute of "statement". It is also permissible for it to be related to "yu'minun" (they believe), placed first for the sake of the fasila (verse-end rhyme).

Ibn 'Amir, Abu Bakr, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿tu'minun﴾ with the upper ta' (second person), and this agrees with His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and in your creation﴾ according to the apparent and the form; otherwise, what is intended here is the disbelievers, contrary to that.

Talha read ﴿tuqinun﴾ with the upper ta' and the qaf, from al-iqan (certainty).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 7:

﴿Woe to every sinful liar﴾ who utters much falsehood, i.e., much lying, ﴿sinful﴾ who commits much sin. The verse was revealed concerning Abu Jahl. It was also said that it was revealed concerning al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who used to purchase tales of the non-Arabs (al-a'ajim) and occupy people with them, distracting them from listening to the Qur'an. However, it is general (ʿāmm) in application, as the wording (muqtada kull) indicates, and whoever it was revealed about enters it as a primary inclusion. And ﴿أثِيمٍ﴾ (atheem, "sinful") is a qualifier (sifah) of ﴿أفّاكٍ﴾ (affaak, "liar").

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on surah 45, verse 8:

"His saying, ﴿hearing the signs of Allah﴾, is another attribute of him. It has been said that it is a new sentence (isti'naf), and it has been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in ﴿sinful﴾."

Page 143

"His saying, glorified is He, ﴿which are recited to him﴾, is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to ﴿the signs of Allah﴾. It was not permitted to make it a second object of ﴿hearing﴾, because the condition for that is that what follows it be something that is not heard, as in 'I heard Zayd reciting.' The apparent meaning of ﴿are recited﴾ is continuity, because that is what suits the sense of disapproval (istib'ad) indicated by His saying, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿then he persists﴾. For ﴿thumma﴾ (then) here indicates the remoteness of persisting after hearing the signs, and it is for graduated sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi). It is possible to keep it in its literal sense, except that the first reading is more eloquent and better suited to the context. A parallel to this use of remoteness is the verse of Ja'far ibn 'Aliyya:

'None removes the dire distress except the son of a free woman,
who sees the surges of death and then visits them.'

Persisting in something (al-israr 'ala al-shay') means adhering to it and not parting from it. It derives from sarr (sharr), meaning to tighten, and from it comes surrat al-darahim (a bag of coins). It is said: 'The donkey shrank (sarra) its ears', meaning it pressed them flat, and 'the donkey asarra' [in the sense of pressing its ears], and one does not say 'asarra udhunayhi' according to what is in al-Sihah. It seems that its meaning then is 'it became one who presses its ears'.

The meaning here is: ﴿then he persists﴾ in his unbelief and error, ﴿being arrogant﴾ toward faith in the signs. ﴿Arrogant﴾ is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿persists﴾. His saying, glorified is He, ﴿as if he had not heard them﴾, is a circumstantial clause after a circumstantial clause, or a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in ﴿arrogant﴾. A new sentence was also permitted. ﴿Ka'anna﴾ (as if) is the lightened form of ka'anna, with one of the two nuns deleted, and its subject is the pronoun of the matter (damir al-sha'n). It has been said that there is no need to estimate it, as is the case with the open-form anna. The meaning is: he persists, arrogant, like one who did not hear them. ﴿So give him the good tidings of a painful punishment﴾ for his persistence in that. Good tidings (bishara) originally means news that changes the color of the skin, whether good or bad, but common usage restricted it to joyful news. If the customary meaning is intended, then it is an ironic metaphor (isti'ara tahakkumiyya), or it is of the type of:

'Their greeting among them is a painful blow.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 9:

﴿And when he learns of any of Our signs﴾ — that is, when news of some of Our signs reaches him and he knows that it is from them.

﴿he takes them in mockery﴾ — he hastens to mock all the signs, and does not restrict his mockery to what has reached him. It is also permissible that the meaning is: when he learns of any of Our signs something that the stubborn opponent can cling to, and find in it a pretext by which he climbs up to attack and find fault, he seizes upon it and takes the signs of Allah Most High in mockery. This is like the objection of Ibn al-Zib'ara to the words of Allah Most High, ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are fuel for Hell﴾, and his sophistry toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and his saying, according to some narrations: "I have bested you." So the pronoun in ﴿took them﴾ refers to the signs on both interpretations. The difference between the two is that ﴿any﴾ in the second has a restriction, due to the indication of ﴿took them in mockery﴾, since it admits only what could be imagined to bear that, and then he makes it a rule for the rest, saying, "All of it is of this kind." There is also a difference between the two interpretations in that in the first, the taking (of them in mockery) is before reflection, while in the second it is after reflection and after distinguishing one sign from another. It has been said: the mockery is of what he knew of the signs, but he returned the pronoun to the signs because mockery of one of them is mockery of all of them, due to their similarity. It is also permissible that the pronoun refers to "shay'" (thing), and the feminine form is used because it carries the meaning of "ayah" (sign), as in the saying of Abu al-'Atahiyya:

My soul is suspended with something of this world — Allah, and the rightly guided Caliph al-Mahdi, suffice it.

He means by "shay'" the threshold of a slave-girl of al-Mahdi's from among his concubines, whom Abu al-'Atahiyya loved, and so he said what he said.

Qatada and Matar al-Warraq read (ʿullima) with a damma on the ʿayn and a shadda on the lam, in the passive voice.

﴿Those﴾ — a demonstrative referring to every liar (affik) insofar as he is characterized by what has been mentioned of the vile traits; the plural is used in view of its inclusion of all of them, as in the words of Allah Most High, ﴿every party rejoicing in what it has﴾, just as the singular is used in the pronouns mentioned earlier with regard to each one individually. The distal particle indicates the remoteness of their rank in evil.

﴿For them﴾ — because of their aforementioned misdeeds, ﴿is a humiliating punishment﴾. He described the punishment as humiliating in order to give full due to their arrogance and their mockery of the signs of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 10:

﴿Before them is Hell﴾, that is, in front of them, since they are turning toward it; or ﴿behind them﴾, since they turn away from paying heed to it and from occupying themselves with what would save them from it, being devoted to this world and immersed in its desires. The word al-waraʾ (behind/beyond) is used in both these senses, because it is the name of the direction which a person conceals himself from, so it encompasses both the back and the front. It has been said, regarding the justification for the sense of "behind," that since Hell would become real for them after their term, it was made as if it were behind them. ﴿And none of what they earned will avail them﴾, meaning, will not repel, ﴿anything﴾ of the punishment of Allah, the Exalted, that is, what they earned of wealth and children; or anything of benefit, with ﴿anything﴾ being either the direct object or the absolute object (object of the verbal noun). ﴿Nor those they took as protectors besides Allah﴾, meaning, what they took, namely the idols.

It is permitted that ﴿mā﴾ be interpreted as encompassing them and all other false objects of worship. The first (interpretation) is more apparent. It is also permitted that ﴿mā﴾ in both places be a verbal (maṣdariyya) particle. The placement of the two negative particles between the two conjoined elements, although the non-benefit of the idols is more evident and clearer than the non-benefit of wealth and children, is definitive, based on their corrupt assumption, since they used to hope for their intercession; and in it is mockery. ﴿And for them﴾, in what lies behind them of Hell, ﴿is a great punishment﴾ whose extent cannot be measured.

﴿This﴾, that is, the Qur'an, as indicated by what follows and by what precedes it: ﴿hears the signs of Allah﴾. And when he knows of Our signs.

﴿These are the signs of Allah, which We recite to you﴾ ﴿as guidance﴾, in the utmost perfection of guidance, as if it were guidance itself. ﴿But those who disbelieve in the signs of their Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an too, on the basis that the idafa (genitive construction) is one of specific reference (li-l-'ahd). The apparent expression would have been the pronoun, but it was replaced with what is in the sublime arrangement, to intensify the ugliness of their disbelief in it and the horror of their condition. It is also permitted that by "the signs" is meant what includes the Qur'an and other than it.

﴿For them is a punishment of a painful kind (rijz)﴾, of the most severe punishment. ﴿Alim﴾ with the nominative (رفع) is an adjective of ﴿punishment (ʿadhab)﴾, placed later for the sake of the fasila (verse-ending rhyme).

Some of the Seven Readers (al-Sab'a) read ﴿ألِيمٍ﴾ with the genitive (جر), as an adjective of ﴿rijz﴾. Making it an adjective of ﴿ʿadhab﴾ as well, with the genitive by mujawara (attraction through proximity), is not something to be given attention. It has been said: according to the reading with the nominative, the word ﴿الرِّجْزُ﴾ (rijz) has the meaning of ﴿الرِّجْسُ﴾ (rijs), which is filth, and the meaning is: for them is a painful punishment from swallowing filth or drinking filth, and what is meant by it is the pus that the disbeliever swallows and can hardly get down. There is no need for this, as is not hidden. The tanwin of ﴿ʿadhab﴾ in all three positions is for magnification (tafkhim). Its nominative is either as the subject of a nominal sentence (ibtida') or as the agent (fa'iliyya) of the adverbial phrase (zarf).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 12:

﴿It is Allah who subjected the sea to you﴾ by making it smooth on its surface, so that things that are light, like wood, float upon it, and it does not prevent diving into it. ﴿That the ships may run upon it by His command﴾ — by His subjecting it [to them] and facilitating their use for what they are intended for. It has also been said: by His creating [it] or by His permission, mighty and majestic is He. The context of the favour (imtinan) requires that the meaning be: that the ships may run upon it while you are riding them.

﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ through trade, diving, hunting and other things, ﴿and that you may be grateful﴾, and so that you may give thanks for the blessings that follow from that. This — I mean ﴿It is Allah who subjected﴾ up to the end — is mentioned as a completion of the rebuke (taqri'), and for this reason the immediate benefits are mentioned after it, for it generally demands gratitude even from the disbeliever. So it is as if it were said: those signs are more worthy of gratitude. For this reason he follows it with what encompasses both categories, namely

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 13:

His statement, glorified is He: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, meaning of the existent things, by placing in them benefits for you from them, some apparent and some hidden. He follows it with reflection (tafakkur) to alert that it is reflection which leads to what has been mentioned of priority, and to indicate that reflection is the criterion of the matter in arranging the purpose upon what has been made a sign of faith, certainty (iman and iqan) and gratitude. ﴿All of it﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal)
Page 145
from ﴿whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾, or an emphasis of it. His statement, exalted is He: ﴿from Him﴾ is also a circumstantial clause from that. The meaning: He subjected these things, all of them, being from Him and originating from Him, meaning that He, glorified is He, is their originator and creator by His power and wisdom, and then their subjector for His creation. Other possibilities have also been permitted regarding it. The first is that it be the predicate of an omitted subject, so "all of it" is then said to be a circumstantial clause of the pronoun hidden in the prepositional phrase, based on the permissibility of placing the circumstantial clause before this kind of governing element, or from the subject, based on permitting a circumstantial clause from it, i.e., they are all from Him, exalted is He. It was also said: "all of it" remains as it was and is considered in shaping the meaning; the subject pronoun is then estimated after it, and its return to what preceded is considered with the restriction "all of it." The sentence, according to both opinions, is a resumptive sentence brought as emphasis of His statement, exalted is He: ﴿subjected﴾, i.e., that He, mighty and majestic, brought them into existence and then subjected them, not that they came to Him from elsewhere, as with kings. The second is that ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ be made the subject, its predicate being it, and ﴿all of it﴾ a circumstantial clause of the pronoun hidden in the prepositional phrase that falls as a relative clause, and ﴿and He has subjected to you﴾ be an emphasis of the first, i.e., He subjected and subjected; and in the conjunction there is an indication that the second subjection is as though it were other than the first, indicating that the one who reflects, whenever he reflects, increases in faith through the perfection of the subjection and the favor upon him. The clause ﴿whatever is in the heavens﴾ and so on is a resumptive sentence for further explanation of the power and wisdom. 

It was objected that if the linguistic emphasis (al-ta'kid al-lughawi) is intended, it is not free from weakness, because conjoining the like of it in sentences is not customary; and if the technical emphasis (al-ta'kid al-istilahi) is intended, as was said regarding His statement: ﴿No! You will soon know. Then no! You will soon know﴾, then it contradicts what Ibn Malik mentioned in al-Tashil, that conjoining emphasis is specific to thumma. Al-Radi said it may also be with fa', and here it is with waw, and none of them permitted it, though they did not mention the reason for the distinction. Moreover, it has been established in the science of meanings (ma'ani) that conjunction does not operate in emphasis at all, due to the strength of connection. It was also objected that this involves omitting the object of ﴿subjected﴾ without any indication, and this, as you see, is weak. The third is that "whatever is on the earth" be the subject and ﴿from Him﴾ its predicate; there is no concealing that this is weak according to the context.

Ibn al-Mundhir related through the chain of Ikrimah that Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, did not used to interpret this verse. Perhaps, if it is authentic, it means that he did not extend discussion on it, for Ibn Jarir related from him that he said concerning it: everything is from Allah, mighty and majestic.

Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related from Tawus who said: A man came to Abdullah ibn Amr ibn al-As and asked him: "Of what was creation created?" He said: "From water, light, darkness, wind, and earth." He said: "Of what were these created?" He said: "I do not know." Then the man went to Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr and asked him, and he said the like of what Abdullah ibn Amr said. Then he went to Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, and asked him: "Of what was creation created?" He said: "From water, light, darkness, wind, and earth." He said: "Of what were these created?" Ibn Abbas then recited: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, all of it from Him﴾. The man said: "None would come with this except a man from the People of the House of the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him."

The scholars differed about what Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, intended by this. Al-Bayhaqi said: he intended that the source of all is from Him, exalted is He, i.e., from His creation, origination and invention. He created water first, or water and what He willed of His creation, mighty and majestic, not from a root nor from a pattern that preceded; then He made it, exalted is He, a root for what He created afterward. So He, exalted is His majesty, is the Originator, and He, glorified is He, is the Creator; there is no god other than Him and no creator besides Him. End. Upon this is the consensus of the muhaddithun, the mufassirun, and those who follow their way. The Shaykh Ibrahim al-Kurani, from the Sufis, said: created things are the determinations (ta'ayyunat) of the emanated existence, which is the form of the Compassionate Self, called al-Ama'; this is because al-Ama' has extended over realities, which are distinct non-existent matters in reality itself. The extension is originated, and al-Ama', from the aspect of its conjunction with quiddities, is other than the Essence of the Truth, exalted is He, for He, glorified is He, is pure Existence not conjoined with them. So existent things are forms originated in al-Ama', subsisting by it, and Allah, exalted is He, is their Sustainer, for He, majestic and exalted, is the First, the Hidden, who sustains those forms with continuance. This does not entail that originated things subsist in the Essence of the Truth, exalted is He, nor that He, glorified is He, is their matter, for His existence, exalted is He, is abstracted from quiddities and not conjoined with them; and what is determined according to them is al-Ama', which is the existence emanated from Him, exalted is He, by His bringing it into being, majestic is His majesty. By this, the answer to the question fits without strain or danger. Had Ibn Abbas's intent been merely what al-Bayhaqi mentioned, that the source of all is from His creation, exalted is He, the statement of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾ would have sufficed for that. But the question was asked with "of what," and the answer came with "from Him" in his recitation of the verse. So it is apparent that what the questioner understood from his recitation, may Allah be pleased with him, is not merely what was mentioned, as shown by his praise with the words: "None would come with this," and so on. For what al-Bayhaqi mentioned is known to everyone who believes in the statement of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Allah is the Creator of everything﴾. Then there appears no basis for the answer of each of Ibn Amr and Ibn al-Zubayr, "I do not know," for both are among the best of believers in the fact that Allah, exalted is He, is the Creator of everything. Rather, what he understood is what we have pointed to. End. Upon this is the general body of the people of Unity (ahl al-wahdah). (The first group) answered that Ibn Abbas's intent was to cut off the infinite regress in questioning, after mention of matter for some things, by stating that the final matter is that all things were created by His power, exalted is He, not from anything; and this is a wise statement whose speaker is praised, which Ibn al-Zubayr and Ibn Amr did not reach. This is not disturbed by His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Or were they created from nothing?﴾, because of what the exegetes said about it, and it will come, Allah willing, in its place. So reflect on that, and may Allah, exalted is He, guide you. Al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Waqid, in the assembly of al-Rashid, cited this verse in refutation of a Christian who claimed that His statement, exalted is He, about Isa, peace be upon him: ﴿and a spirit from Him﴾ indicates what he claimed about him, peace be upon him, that he is the son of Allah, glorified and exalted is He above what they describe.

Abu al-Fath and the author of al-Lawami related from Ibn Abbas, Abdullah ibn Amr, al-Jahdari, and Abdullah ibn Ubayd ibn Umayr that they recited (minnatan) with a kasra on the mim, a shadda on the nun, and a fatha on the ta', as an object of purpose, meaning: He subjected that to you as a favor upon you. Ibn Khalawayh also related it from Ibn Abbas. But Abu Hatim said: its chain to him is obscure. If the chain is sound, it may be said regarding the previously mentioned narration of Tawus that he recited the verse according to the reading of the majority, and it is possible that he had two readings for it.

Maslama ibn Muharib recited likewise, except that he put a damma on the ta', as an estimate of "it is" or "she is" a favor. Also from him: a fatha on the mim, a shadda on the nun, and the written ha' referring to Allah, exalted is He, meaning: His bounty, and He is the agent of ﴿subjected﴾ by metaphorical attribution, as you say: "The generosity of the king has uplifted me." Or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: this, or it is from Him, exalted is He. Agency has been permitted in his first reading. The masculine verb is used because the agent is not a true feminine, with the separation present. The first aspect is better, though it involves an estimate.

﴿Indeed in that﴾, i.e., in what has been mentioned, ﴿are signs﴾ of great importance and great number, ﴿for a people who reflect﴾ upon the wonders of His creation and the greatness of His majestic affairs, for that leads them to faith, certainty, and gratitude.

[Page 147]

The object of "say" is omitted, because "forgive" (yaghfiru) indicates it. The verb "yaghfiru" is a response to the command (jawab al-amr, the answer to an imperative), in terms of its connection to the command and not in terms of itself alone. The meaning is: say to them, "Forgive, and they will forgive." ﴿For those who do not expect the days of Allah﴾ means: those who do not hope for, that is, who do not expect, forgive and overlook. "Those who do not expect His events" refers to the events that Allah brings about against His enemies and His vengeance upon them. "Hope" (yarjuna) is used figuratively for "expect" (tawaqqu'), and likewise "days" (ayyam) is figurative for "events" (waqai'), from the expression of the Arabs, "the days of the Arabs" meaning their battles. This is a well-known figurative usage, and it is narrated from Mujahid (Mujahid ibn Jabr). Or the meaning is: those who do not look forward to the times that Allah has appointed for the reward of the believers and promised them victory in them.

It is said that the verse was revealed before the verse of fighting (qital), and then it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation) by it.

Some scholars said: there is no abrogation, because what is meant here is leaving off disputes over trivial matters and overlooking some things that cause harm and distress. This is related by al-Nahhas (Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas) and al-Mahdawi (Abu al-'Abbas al-Mahdawi), from Ibn Abbas (Abdullah ibn Abbas), that the verse was revealed concerning Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: a polytheist in Makkah reviled him before the Hijrah, so he intended to strike him, and then the verse was revealed. This is also narrated from Muqatil (Muqatil ibn Sulayman). This clearly indicates that the verse is Meccan, like its companions. The intention that he meant to strike him after the Hijrah is not likely, because the Muslims in Makkah before it were helpless and oppressed, and they could not avenge themselves against the polytheists, and the helpless person is not commanded to pardon and overlook. The claim that the continuation of each Muslim's helplessness is not known is not clear and requires a transmission. Rather, whoever knows the circumstances of Abu Hafs, may Allah be pleased with him, does not doubt that he was able to do what he intended, without caring about its consequences.

This is better as an answer than to say that the command to do that is between him and Allah in his heart, so that he may be rewarded for it. However, it has been said that the Prophet (ﷺ) and his companions camped at a well called al-Muraysi' during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq. Ibn Ubayy sent his servant to draw water, and he was slow. When he came to him, he said: "What kept you?" He said: "The servant of Umar sat at the edge of the well and did not let anyone draw water until he filled the waterskins of the Prophet (ﷺ) and the waterskin of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him." So Ibn Ubayy said: "We and these people are only like what is said: 'Fatten your dog and it will devour you.'" This reached Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he drew his sword, intending to go to him. Then Allah revealed the verse. The Imam (al-Razi) related this from Ibn Abbas, and it indicates that it is Medinan. Likewise is what is narrated from Maymun ibn Mihran, who said: Finhas the Jew said: "When Allah revealed ﴿Who is it that will lend Allah a goodly loan?﴾, the Lord of Muhammad became needy." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, heard of this, drew his sword and went out. The Prophet (ﷺ) sent for him until he brought him back, and the verse was revealed: ﴿so that He may recompense a people for what they used to earn﴾. This is the reason for the command to forgive. It is also permitted that it is the reason for the command to speak, because it is a cause for their compliance, for which they are recompensed. The "people" (qawm) here means the believers who forgive. The indefiniteness (tankir) of "qawm" is for magnification. The word "qawm" in itself is a term of praise, as derivation and usage indicate, as in the phrase "O son of the people" (ya ibna al-qawm).

In this indefiniteness is complete clarity and an alert that they are not hidden, whether they are indefinite or definite, together with the knowledge that the one who is recompensed is only the doer, and here that is the forgiver. That is, they were commanded to this so that Allah may recompense on the Day of Resurrection a people, any people whatsoever, and specific people for what they earned in this world of good deeds, among which is patience with the harm of the disbelievers and turning away from them by swallowing anger and bearing what is disliked, with a great reward that the scope of explanation cannot encompass. Some restricted what they earned to forgiveness and patience with harm. In both interpretations, ما (ma) is a relative pronoun. It is also permitted that it be a verbal-noun particle (masdariyyah), and the ba' is causal (sababiyyah), or for exchange (muqabalah), or it is related to "yajzi" (the verb of recompense).

It is also permitted that "qawm" refers to the disbelievers, and "what they earned" refers to their evil deeds, among which is their harming of the believers. The indefiniteness is for belittlement. It has been criticized: the absolute recompense is not suitable as the reason for the command to forgive, because it occurs under both the assumption of forgiveness and its absence. Therefore it must be restricted to the whole, such that none of it is realized in this world, or to what proceeds from Allah Himself. In this there is much strained interpretation, which is not hidden. It is also permitted that both groups are meant, and the indefiniteness is for generality. This has been criticized as being more strained and far-fetched. What supports the first interpretation is what is narrated from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, who said: "We were before Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and a reciter recited this verse, so he said: 'Let it recompense Umar for what he did.'"

Zayd ibn Ali, Abu Abd al-Rahman, al-A'mash, Abu Khulayd, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read (linajziya) with the nun of majesty (nun al-'azamah, the first-person plural "we"). It is also read (liyujza) with the ya' and in the passive voice (al-bina' lil-maf'ul), with "qawmun" in the nominative, as the substitute for the agent (na'ib al-fa'il). Shayba and Abu Ja'far, with a difference of narration from him, read it likewise, except that they both put "qawman" in the accusative. This is narrated from Asim. Those who permit the substitution of a prepositional phrase for the agent even when there is an explicit object (maf'ul sarih) use it as evidence, and say: "It was struck with a whip, Zayd" (duriba bi-sawtin Zaydan). Thus "bi-ma kasabu" is the substitute for the agent here. The majority do not permit this. This reading is explained as follows: the pronoun standing in place of the agent is the pronoun of the verbal noun, meaning "liyujza huwa", that is, "the recompense" (al-jaza'). It is refuted that it is not substituted in place of it when there is also an object (maf'ul bihi), according to the correct view. The Kufians permitted it, with disagreement about its absolute permissibility and its preference. Or the pronoun is that of the second object, which is "the recompense," meaning "the thing recompensed with," as in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Their reward with their Lord is Gardens of Eden﴾. It is omitted because the context indicates it, as in His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and for his parents﴾. The second object in the chapter of "a'ta" (to give) takes the place of the agent without disagreement, and this is of that type. Abu al-Baqa' considered "al-khayr" (good) as a substitute for the mentioned recompense. Or "qawman" is in the accusative by an implied "a'ni" (I mean), or the verb "jaza" is implied, indicated by the passive, meaning that there is a recompenser. Abu Hayyan chose this view. In that case "liyajziya" is of the type "yu'tiy" and "yamna'" (the verb with two objects, or the verb meaning to give), and the meaning is: "that he may do the recompense." It is then a matter of two clauses. The phrase "wa hila bayna al-'ir wal-nazawan" (a proverb meaning: a barrier came between them, indicating the impossibility of the matter) is cited here as a parallel.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 15:

﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own soul; and whoever does evil, it is against it.﴾ Action hardly ever passes over to anyone other than its doer. ﴿Then to your Lord﴾, the Owner of your affairs, ﴿you will be returned﴾, so that He will recompense you for your deeds as wisdom requires: good for good and evil for evil. The sentence is a fresh (mustanf'a) clause explaining the manner of the recompense.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 16:

﴿And We certainly gave the Children of Israel the Book﴾ — namely the Torah. This is on the reading that the definite article (al-) is for a specific known referent (al-ta'rif li-l-'ahd). It is also permissible to take it as generic (li-l-jins), so that it includes the Psalms (al-Zabur) and the Gospel (al-Injil). That the Psalms consist of supplications and intimate prayer, and that the rulings in the Gospel are very few, while most of the rulings of ʿIsa (peace be upon him) come from the Torah, does not harm this reading, because the giving of a Book in general is a favour (minnah). ﴿And the judgment﴾ — that is, the authority to judge and to settle affairs among people, since kingship existed among them; this is the view chosen by Abu Hayyan. Or it means understanding (fiqh) in religion; it is said: the understanding of rulings was never as extensive given to any prophet as it was through the tongue of Musa (peace be upon him). Or it means wisdom (hikam), both the theoretical principles (al-nazariyyah al-asliyyah) and the practical branches (al-'amaliyyah al-far'iyyah). ﴿And prophethood﴾ — since many prophets (peace be upon them) arose among them, more than arose among any other people. ﴿And We provided them with good things﴾ — pleasant lawful things, and by this blessing is completed; this refers to such things as the manna and the quails. ﴿And We preferred them over the worlds﴾ — since We gave them what We did not give others, such as the splitting of the sea and the shading of the cloud and similar things. So the intended meaning is their preference over the worlds in an absolute sense, but only in some respects, not in all of them, and not in terms of rank and reward. Thus this does not contradict the preference of the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ) over them in another respect, namely in rank and reward. It has been said that "the worlds" here means the worlds of their own time.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 17:

﴿And We gave them clear proofs concerning the matter﴾ — clear evidences in the matter of the religion. Here "min" (مِن) carries the sense of "in" (فِي), and "bayyināt" (بَيِّنات) means proofs. Among them are the miracles of Musa, peace be upon him, and some have explained it as referring to these alone. And it is related from Ibn ʿAbbas (رضي الله عنهما) that they are signs concerning the affair of the Prophet (ﷺ) and clear indications of his truthfulness, peace be upon him, such as his emigrating from Makkah to Yathrib and his having its people as his helpers, and other things that were mentioned in their books.

﴿So they did not differ﴾ concerning that matter ﴿except after knowledge had come to them﴾ of the reality of the situation. Thus they made that which should cause the disappearance of disagreement a cause for its firm establishment. ﴿Out of envy among themselves﴾ — enmity and jealousy, not doubt about it. ﴿Indeed your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ by way of requital and recompense ﴿concerning that about which they used to differ﴾ — concerning the matter of the religion.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 18:

﴿Then We placed you on a path (sharia)﴾ That is, a sunnah and a way, from shara'ahu (he laid it down) when he prescribed it, so that it may be followed. In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit): in the speech of the Arabs, the shari'a (watering place, a path to water) is the place from which people approach rivers and the like.

Page 149

So the sharia of the religion derives from this, from the point from which people approach it, namely the command of God Most High, His mercy, and nearness to Him, mighty and majestic. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said: al-shar' is a verbal noun, then it became a name for the clear, plain path, so it is said shar', shir'a and shari'a. This was borrowed for the divine way of religion. Then he said: Some have said the sharia was called sharia by analogy with the sharia of water, in that whoever approaches it in truth and sincerity is quenched and purified. By quenching I mean what one of the wise said: "I used to drink and was not satisfied; when I came to know God Most High, I was satisfied without drinking." By purification I mean what He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Allah only desires to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you thoroughly﴾. The apparent meaning here is the linguistic meaning. The tanwin (indefiniteness) is for glorification, meaning a sharia of great standing. ﴿of the matter﴾ That is, the matter of religion. Abu Hayyan allowed that it is a verbal noun of amr, and the intended meaning is of command and prohibition, and it is, as you see, far-fetched. ﴿So follow it, and do not follow the desires of those who do not know﴾ That is, the opinions of the ignorant that follow appetites. The intended ones include every deviant. It was said: they are the ignorant among Qurayza and al-Nadir. It was said: they are the leaders of Quraysh who used to say to him (ﷺ): "Return to the religion of your fathers."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 19:

﴿Indeed, they will never avail you against Allah in anything.﴾ "Shay'an" (anything) may mean "from among things," or it may mean "a share of benefit (ighna')," meaning: "if I followed them." The sentence is resumptive (mustanaffa'ah), explaining the reason for the prohibition. ﴿And indeed, the wrongdoers are allies of one another.﴾ He does not take them as allies, nor does he follow their desires, except one who is a wrongdoer like them.

﴿And Allah is the Ally of the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾ — those whom you are a model for. So persist in what you are upon, of turning to Him, glorified is He, alone, and turning away from all else, mighty and majestic is He, completely.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 20:

﴿This﴾, i.e., the Qur'an, ﴿is insight for mankind﴾. For what it contains of the landmarks of the religion (ma'alim al-din) and the rites of the laws (sha'a'ir al-shara'i') is in the position of insights in the hearts. It has also been said: the reference is to following the Sharia, and the speech is of the type of eloquent metaphor (al-tashbih al-baligh). The predicate is given in the plural in both readings, in consideration of the multiplicity of what the subject includes, and the following of a verbal noun in the genitive construction (idafa) makes it general, so it also informs about it with a plural. It is also read as ﴿هَذِهِ﴾ (hadhihi, "these"), i.e., the verses. ﴿And guidance﴾, sublime, from the pit of misguidance, ﴿and mercy﴾, great, ﴿for a people who are certain﴾, for whom certainty in matters is a characteristic.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 21:

﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think﴾ ... to the end of the verse. This is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf) brought to explain the condition of the evildoers and the righteous, following the explanation of the condition of the wrongdoers and the God-fearing. The particle ﴿أم﴾ (am) is disjunctive (munqati'ah), and what it contains of the meaning of ﴿بل﴾ (bal, "rather") serves to shift from the first explanation to the second. The interrogative hamzah is for the denial of the supposition, meaning that it is not fitting or proper, since its opposite is evident. Al-ijtirah (اجترح) means al-iktisab (acquiring). From it comes al-jarihah (الجارحة), the limbs through which one acquires, such as the hands. It is said: "He is the jarihah of his family," meaning their earner. Al-Raghib said: al-ijtirah is the acquiring of sin, and its root is from al-jirahah (wound), just as al-iqtiraf (اقتراف) is from qaraf al-qarhah (the scab of a wound). The apparent sense here is to interpret it as acquiring, because of ﴿السيئات﴾ (the evil deeds). According to al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit), what is meant by them is the evil deeds of disbelief. His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿أن نجعلهم﴾ (that We should make them) fills the place of the two objects of the verb ḥasiba (to suppose). Al-ja'l (الجعل) here means al-tasyir (to make into). ﴿Them﴾ is its first object, and His, the Glorified's, saying ﴿كالذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات﴾ (like those who believed and did righteous deeds) is its second object. His, the Mighty and Majestic's, saying ﴿سواء﴾ (equal) is a substitute (badal) for the kaf (ك, "like") on the basis that it is a noun with the meaning of "mithl" (مثل, "like"). His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿محياهم ومماتهم﴾ (their living and their dying) is the subject (fa'il) of sawa', treated as if it were mustawin (equal), as they say: "I passed by a man who is sawa' [equal] with the nonexistent (al-'adam)." The plural pronoun refers to those who committed evil. The meaning, on the denial of the supposition, is that the living and dying of those who committed evil are equal to those of the believers. The object of the denial is the equality of that, for the believers' conditions correspond, since they are shown mercy in life and in death, whereas those (the evildoers) have opposite conditions, for they are shown mercy in life but not in death. It is also permissible that ﴿سواء﴾ be a circumstantial state (hal) from the pronoun in the kaf, on the basis of the meaning you have heard.

[Page 150]

It has been objected that it is a fixed noun in the form of a particle, so a hidden pronoun cannot be in it, and al-Farisi (الفارسي) explicitly prohibited that. Yes, it is permissible that ﴿كالذين﴾ be a prepositional phrase in the place of the second object, and ﴿سواء﴾ a state (hal) from the hidden pronoun within it. It was also said: it is permissible that it be a state from the pronoun in ﴿نجعلهم﴾ (We make them), and likewise it is permissible that it be the second object, and that the kaf or the prepositional phrase be a state from this pronoun. What was mentioned first is more apparent and preferable. It is also permissible that the plural pronoun in ﴿محياهم ومماتهم﴾ refers to the believers, so that ﴿سواء﴾ is a state from the second relative pronoun (al-mawsul al-thani). It is not permissible that it be a state from the pronoun in ﴿كالذين﴾, because of the corruption of the meaning, and because the pronoun refers to the two groups, so ﴿سواء﴾ is a state from the whole of the second relative pronoun and the first pronoun. The meaning, on the denial of the supposition that the two groups are equal after death in honor or in the abandonment of punishment, is as they were apparently equal in provision and health in life. It is also permissible that the meaning, on the denial of the supposition that the two lives are made equal, is that the believers are on obedience and those (the evildoers) are on sins, and likewise the two deaths, because the believers are met with glad tidings and pleasure, and those with evil and abandonment. It was said that this applies also on the assumption that the pronoun refers to those who committed evil.

It has been asked why the verifier (al-Mudaqqiq) did not permit the substitution for the kaf on the assumption that the pronoun is shared, since "mithl" (likeness) is the thing compared and ﴿سواء﴾ applies to both the compared and the thing it is compared to.

Most of the reciters read ﴿سواءٌ محياهم ومماتهم﴾ with the nominative (raf') on ﴿سواءٌ﴾ and what follows it, on the basis that ﴿سواءٌ﴾ is a predicate placed first (khabar muqaddam) and what follows it is the subject (mubtada'), not the reverse, because ﴿سواء﴾ is indefinite (nakirah) and there is no justification for beginning with it. The pronoun refers to those who committed evil. The sentence, it was said, is a substitute (badal) for the second object of ﴿نجعل﴾ (We make): a substitute of the whole for the whole (badal kull min kull), or a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal), or a substitute of a part (badal ba'd). In any case, it involves the substitution of a sentence for a single word (idbal al-jumlah min al-mufrad). Abu al-Fath (أبو الفتح) permitted it, and Ibn Malik chose it and cited evidences for it. Abu Hayyan said: the substitution is not definitely required here. Muhammad ibn 'Abd Allah al-Ishbili, known as Ibn al-'Ilj, said in his book al-Basit fi al-Nahw: it is not valid for a sentence that is governed by the first to be in the place of a substitute; if it is not governed, then is it a sentence substituting for a sentence? In my view it is not far from permissible, like conjunction and verbal emphasis.

Its apparent meaning is that substitution is not permitted here. In al-Bahr it appears to me that it is not permitted to substitute this sentence for that object, because al-ja'l here means al-tasyir (making into), and one does not say "I made Zayd his father is standing" or "I made Zayd his slave is departing," because that involves a transition from one essence to another essence, or from an attribute of the essences to another attribute in them, whereas in that supposed sentence, as a second object, there is no transition from what we mentioned. There is a discussion here that is not hidden. Al-Zamakhshari (الزمخشري) explicitly stated that the sentence is a substitute for the kaf, and he is an imam in Arabic. However, the author of al-Kashf (صاحب الكشف) clarified that he meant that it is a substitute in terms of meaning, not that it is a substitute for that in wording. He said: because that is a single word indicating the essence in terms of meaning, whereas this indicates the meaning, even though the essence necessarily follows from it, unless one supposes for it an omitted modifier, such that one supposes "men, equal are their living and their dying," for example. The meaning on the substitution reading is as you have heard in the accusative reading. It is also permissible that the sentence be a second object and ﴿كالذين﴾ a state from the pronoun in ﴿نجعلهم﴾. What is for and against this is not hidden from you. If the pronoun refers to the believers, then the sentence is said to be a state from the second relative pronoun, not from the pronoun in the second object, because of the corruption (of the meaning). It has been objected that this involves the nominal state clause (al-jumlah al-ismiyyah al-haliyyah) being satisfied by the pronoun alone, which is not eloquent, according to what has been said. It was also said: it is a resumptive sentence explaining the reason for the denial of the supposition of similarity, namely that the believers are equal in their condition before God in both abodes, in radiance and honor, so how could those who committed evil be like them? It is permissible that it be an explanation of the aspect of the ambiguous comparison (wajh al-shibh al-mujmal). If the pronoun refers to both groups, then the apparent view is that the sentence is independent speech, not included under the ruling of the denial, and the equality then is between the condition of the believers relative to them specifically and the condition of those who committed evil in the same way. The sentence would then be a justification for the denial in meaning, indicating non-similarity neither in this world nor in the Hereafter, because the believers are equal in living and dying in mercy, and those are equal in living and dying in retribution, since the meaning is: as they live, so they die. Then, since the condition of these differs from the condition of those in life, so likewise [it differs] in death. As for the substitution, its status is known, so reflect.

[Page 151]

Al-A'mash read ﴿سواءً﴾ with the accusative, and ﴿محياهم ومماتهم﴾ with it also. The first was interpreted as you have heard, and the accusative of ﴿محياهم ومماتهم﴾ is adverbial (zarfiyyah), because they are nouns of time, or verbal nouns placed in the position of time, and the governing element is either ﴿سواءً﴾ or ﴿نجعلهم﴾.

This is all. Although the verse concerns the disbelievers, according to what is reported from al-Bahr, and this is the apparent meaning of what is narrated from al-Kalbi, that 'Utbah, Shaybah and al-Walid ibn 'Utbah said to 'Ali, may Allah honor his face, and Hamzah, may Allah be pleased with him, and the believers: "By Allah, you are not upon anything. And if what you say is true, our condition is better than yours in the Hereafter, just as it is better in this world." Then the verse was revealed: ﴿Or do those who commit evil deeds think﴾ and so on.

It contains a refutation of them in all its aspects, as is known by minimal reflection. From it is derived the contrast between the condition of the believer who is disobedient and the believer who is obedient. For this reason many worshippers wept when reciting it, so much so that it is called "the weeping-place of the worshippers" (mabkat al-'abidin) because of this. Abdullah ibn Ahmad in Zawa'id al-Zuhd, al-Tabarani and a group reported from Abu al-Duha, who said: Tamim al-Dari recited Surah al-Jathiyah, and when he reached His, the Exalted's, saying ﴿Or do those who ...﴾, the verse, he kept repeating it and weeping until morning, while he was at the Maqam.

Ibn Abi Shaybah reported from Bashir, the client of al-Rabi' ibn Khaytham, that al-Rabi' was praying, and passed by this verse ﴿Or do those who ...﴾ and so on, and he kept repeating it until morning. Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad used to say to himself when he recited it: "I wish I knew which of the two groups you are from."

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: its wording indicates that the commission of evil deeds is the commission of disbelief, because it is set in opposition to faith. It is possible, however, that the opposition is between commission (of evil) and doing righteous deeds, with faith being in both groups. For this reason the fearful wept when reciting it.

I have seen many of the deluded, who spend their nights and days in wickedness and immorality, saying with the tongue of speech and the tongue of state: "We will be in a better condition on the Day of Resurrection than many of the worshippers." This, from them, and we seek refuge in Allah the Exalted, is a far error and a delusion beyond which there is no further. ﴿Evil is what they judge﴾, meaning: evil is their judgment, this judgment being the equality. So "ma" is a verbal (masdariyyah) particle, and the statement is an informing about the ugliness of their known judgment.

It is also permissible that it is for the expression of censure of them, on the basis that "saa'" (ساء) has the meaning of "bi's" (بئس, "how evil"). Then "ma" in it is an indefinite descriptive noun that occurs as a specifying explanation (tamyiz) of the ambiguous pronoun of the subject, and the object of the censure is omitted, meaning: "How evil a thing they judged that to be."

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 22:

﴿And Allah created the heavens and the earth with truth﴾. This seems to be a refutation of their earlier supposition, or a proof that the life and death of every group are equal, and an explanation of its wisdom, on the assumption that the words of His, exalted is He, ﴿Their living and their dying are equal﴾ are a resumptive statement (isti'naf). This is because the creation of the world with truth, which requires justice, necessitates that the oppressed be vindicated against the oppressor and that there be a distinction between the evildoer and the doer of good. If there is no distinction in this life, then after death it is inevitable. ﴿And that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned﴾ is conjoined (atf) to ﴿with truth﴾, because it carries the sense of a cause (illah), whether the bi' (ب) is for the final causal sense (al-sababiyyah al-ghda'iyyah) or for accompaniment (al-mulabasah). As for the first, it is clear. As for the second, the meaning is: He created them accompanied and joined with wisdom and rightness, not with futility and falsehood, and the outcome is: He created them for that purpose. Or it is conjoined to a deleted cause, like "so that He, glorified is He, may show by them His power," or "so that He may do justice." The particle ma (ما) is either a relative pronoun (mawsulah) or a verbal-source particle (masdariyyah), meaning: so that He may recompense every soul for that which it has earned, or for its earning. ﴿And they﴾, i.e., the souls implied by "every soul", ﴿will not be wronged﴾ by a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (hal). The naming of that as wronging, although it is not so in reality, is because it is, from Him, glorified is He, a disposal in His own dominion, whereas wronging is the disposal of another's dominion without his permission, since if anyone other than Him, mighty and majestic, did it, it would be wronging. So the discourse is based on the figurative metaphor (al-isti'arah al-tamthiliyyah), or, since it contradicts His true promise, glorified is He, He, exalted is He, named it wronging.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 23:

﴿Have you seen him who has taken his own desire as his god?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at the condition of one who abandoned following guidance for submitting to desire, so that he is as one who worships it. The speech is an elaborate simile (*tashbih baligh*) or a metaphor (*isti'ara*). The *fa'* (فاء) is for coordination (*'atf*) upon an implied antecedent into which the interrogative *hamza* (همزة) entered, meaning: "Have you considered one whose condition is this, and so have you seen him?" For that is among what is marvelled at.

Abu Hayyan made *a-ra'ayta* (أرَأيْتَ) mean "inform me," and said: the first object is *man* (مَنِ) of ﴿*ittakhadha*﴾ (اتَّخَذَ), and the second object is omitted, to be estimated after the relative clauses, meaning: "Would he be guided?" based on the evidence of ﴿So who will guide him?﴾. The verse was revealed, as narrated from Muqatil, concerning al-Harith ibn Qays al-Sahmi, who did not desire anything without mounting it. Its ruling is general, and it contains from the censure of following the desires of the soul what it contains. And from Ibn 'Abbas: Allah did not mention any desire except that He censured it.

Wahb said: "If you are in doubt between two matters, look at the one farther from your desire and go to it." Sahl al-Tustari said: "Your desire is your disease; if you oppose it, it is your cure." And in a hadith: "The incapable one is he who follows his soul's desires and wishes upon Allah, the Exalted."

Abu 'Imran Musa ibn 'Imran al-Ishbili al-Zahid said:

So oppose its desires and disobey it,
for whoever obeys the desire of his soul is brought down to the worst of descents.

And whoever obeys the stubborn soul, it will drive him
and cast him into a fall, what a fall!

This was also censured in the pre-Islamic era, and from it is the saying of 'Antara:

I am a man of gentle disposition, noble,
I do not follow the stubborn soul in its desires.

Perhaps the matter is too clear to need many quotations.

Al-A'raj and Abu Ja'far read ﴿*ilahatan*﴾ (إلَهَةً) with the feminine *ta'* in place of the pronominal *ha'*. And it is narrated from al-A'raj that he read ﴿*alihatan*﴾ (آلِهَةً) in the plural form.

Ibn Khalawayh said: one of them would admire a stone and worship it; when he saw something better than it, he would abandon it, inclining toward the other. Thus the apparent meaning is that *alihatan* (آلِهَةً) is in its literal sense without figurative usage or simile. And *al-hawa* (الهَوى) is in the sense of *al-mahwiyy* (المَهْوِيّ, that which is desired), like his saying:

My desire is with the Yemeni caravan, ascending.

﴿And Allah has sent him astray﴾: that is, He created him astray, or He created misguidance in him, or He forsook him and turned him away from kindness, according to what has been said. ﴿*'ala 'ilm*﴾ (عَلى عِلْمٍ) is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the agent: meaning, Allah, Exalted, sent him astray while knowing, glorified be He, that he was worthy of that because of the corruption of the essence of his soul.

It is permissible that it be a circumstantial clause from the object: meaning, He sent him astray knowing him to be on the path of guidance. This is like His saying, Exalted: ﴿They did not differ except after knowledge had come to them﴾ (45:17).

﴿And He has sealed his hearing and his heart﴾, such that he is not affected by admonitions and does not reflect upon the signs.

﴿And placed upon his sight a covering﴾, preventing him from insight and taking lesson. The speech is figurative (*tamthil*). 'Abdullah and al-A'mash read *ghashawatan* (غَشاوَةً) with a *fatha* on the *ghayn*, which is the dialect of Rabi'a; and al-Hasan, 'Ikrima, 'Abdullah also with a *damma*, which is an 'Ukkali dialect; and Abu Hanifa, Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Talha, and Mas'ud ibn Salih. Al-A'mash also read *ghashwatan* (غَشْوَةً) with a *fatha* on the *ghayn* and sukun on the *shin*; and Ibn Musarrif. Al-A'mash also read it likewise, except that both of them pronounced the *ghayn* with a *kasra*.

﴿So who will guide him after Allah?﴾, meaning: who will guide him after His sending him astray? It was said: the meaning is, who other than Allah, glorified be He, will guide him?

﴿Will you not then be mindful?﴾: that is, will you not take notice, and so be mindful? Al-Jahdari read *tadhkurun* (تَذْكُرُونَ) with the light form, and al-A'mash read *tatadhakkarun* (تَتَذَكَّرُونَ) with two *ta'*s, according to the original form.

[Page 153]

﴿And they say﴾ is an explanation of the firmness of their misguidance, of the sealing over their hearing and their hearts, and of placing a covering over their eyes. The pronoun refers either to "those" (man) according to its meaning, or to the disbelievers. ﴿It is not﴾, that is, what is life, ﴿but our life of this world﴾ in which we are.
