It is permissible that the pronoun refers to the state (al-hal), and the life of this world is one of the states, so the exception is from the same genus as the excepted, since the state of the life of this world is excepted from the most general of states. There is no need to posit a state (hal) with an added noun after the exception particle, that is, "what is the state but the state of the life of this world." ﴿We die and we live﴾ is a judgement about the species as a whole, without consideration of precedence or sequence. However, the placing of "we live" after "we die" in this sublime composition is for the sake of the verse-ending (fasilah, the rhyming close of the verse). That is, a group dies and a group lives, and there is no resurrection at all. It has been said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in the speech, that is, "we live and we die," but this is not the correct view. It has been said that by death they meant the non-existence that precedes the breathing of the spirit into them, that is, "we are sperm-drops and what precedes them and what follows them, and we live after that." It has been said that by life they meant the survival of offspring and progeny, metaphorically, as if they said: "we die by ourselves, and we live through the survival of our children and descendants." It has been said that they meant: some of us die and some of us live, with the figurative usage lying in the attribution. It is also permissible that they meant by life, in a figurative sense, the return of the spirit to another body by way of transmigration (tanasukh, the passing of the soul from body to body), which is the belief of many worshippers of idols, but the remoteness of this is not hidden. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read (wa-nuhya) with a damma on the nun. ﴿And nothing destroys us except time﴾, that is, the lapse of long periods. Thus "dahr" is more specific than "zaman" (time). This is the view preferred by al-Sa'd, and they have a lengthy discussion on this. Al-Raghib said: "Dahr," in origin, is a name for the duration of the world from the beginning of its existence until its ending; then it is used to express any long duration. It is the opposite of "zaman," which applies to both short and long durations. The "dahr" of so-and-so is the duration of his life. It is said: "a calamity befell so-and-so for a dahr," meaning it came down upon him; this was related by al-Khalil. So "dahr" here is a verbal noun (masdar).

Some eminent scholars mentioned that "dahr" in the aforementioned sense is derived from the verbal noun, and that it is said: "dahrahu dahran," meaning he overcame him. Their attribution of destruction to time is a denial on their part of the Angel of Death (Malak al-Mawt) and his taking of souls by the command of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. They used to attribute all events without distinction to it, out of their ignorance that these are decreed by Allah, exalted is He. Their poetry is full of complaints about time, yet these people acknowledge the existence of Allah, exalted is He, so they are not the Dahriyyah (those who hold that time is eternal and the sole agent). For, even though they attribute events to time, they do not affirm the existence of Him, glorified and exalted is He, ﴿Exalted is He far above what they say﴾. Everyone says that time has independent causal efficacy. It is not far-fetched that time, in their view, is the measure of the motion of the celestial sphere, as the majority of philosophers held. It has been reported that there is a prohibition against reviling time.

Muslim (may Allah have mercy on him) reported: "None of you should revile time, for Allah is time," and so did Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, who said: "It is sound according to the condition of Muslim." Allah, Mighty and Majestic, said: "The son of Adam hurts Me, saying: 'O misfortune of time!' Let none of you say: 'O misfortune of time!' For I am time; I turn its night and its day."

Al-Hakim also said, "It is sound according to the condition of Muslim as well," (that) Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: "I have lent to My servant, and he has not lent to Me; My servant reviles Me, and he does not know it, saying: 'Woe is me, O time!' And I am time."

Al-Bayhaqi (reported): "Do not revile time, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: I am the days and the nights; I renew them and wear them out, and I bring kings after kings."

The meaning of this is that Allah, exalted is He, is the one who brings about events. So if you revile time as the agent, the reviling falls upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Some scholars counted reviling it as a grave sin, because it leads to reviling Him, exalted is He, which is disbelief; and whatever leads to it, its lowest degree is that it is disbelief.

The statement of the Shafi'iyyah (the Shafi'i school) is explicit that this is disliked (makruh), not forbidden (haram), let alone a grave sin. What is appropriate in this matter is a distinction: whoever reviles it, if he intends by it the time-period, then there is no question of it being disliked; or if he intends Allah, Mighty and Majestic, then there is no question of it being disbelief. Likewise if he intends the true Effector, for there is none but Allah, glorified is He. But if he uses the term unqualified, then this is the place of doubt, since it may be disbelief or other than that. The apparent sense of their statement here is also disliking, since what is understood from it is the time-period; and its application to Allah, exalted is He, as some eminent scholars said, is only by way of metaphor.

Some people said: its reviling is a grave sin if one believes that it has an effect upon what befalls one, as the ignorant among the Arabs used to believe. There is a question about this, for believing such a thing is disbelief, and the discussion is not about that. Some of them denied that what is in the hadith of Abu Dawud and al-Hakim, "for I am the dahr," is with a damma on the ra'; and he said: if it were so, dahr would be among His names, exalted is He. He would have narrated it as "for I am the dahr" with a fatha on the ra', as an adverbial accusative of time for "I turn," meaning: I turn the night and the day throughout the dahr, that is, over the long lapse of time and its passing. In this there is the point that Muslim's narration "for Allah is the dahr" refutes what he claimed; and for this reason the majority hold the damma on the ra'. It does not follow from this that it is among His names, exalted is He, since it has already been stated that this is by way of metaphor. Al-Raghib related from some of them that the second dahr in Muslim's hadith is other than the first, and that it is a verbal noun in the sense of an active participle, and the meaning is that Allah, exalted is He, is the dahr, that is, the one who causes change, the manager, the one who bestows what occurs. But this is remote.

ʿAbd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read (illa dahrun), and its interpretation: "except a dahr that passes."

﴿And they have no knowledge of that﴾, that is, of what has been mentioned, namely the shortness of life to what is in this world, and the attribution of destruction to time; ﴿of any knowledge﴾ based on reason or transmitted report. ﴿They only conjecture﴾: they are only a people whose utmost concern is conjecture and imitation, without having anything that could in any way be relied upon. This is their corrupt belief about themselves.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 25:**

﴿And when Our verses are recited to them﴾, those which speak the truth, of which resurrection (al-ba'th) is part, ﴿clear﴾, plain in their indication of what they state, which contradicts their belief, or ones that make it clear. ﴿Their argument was only﴾ with the accusative (naṣb), taking it as the predicate (khabar) of kāna (the verbal particle "was") whose subject (ism) is his saying, may He be exalted: ﴿except that they say: "Bring our fathers, if you are truthful"﴾, meaning, regarding our being raised after death. That is, nothing that they held onto was anything other than this false statement, which cannot possibly be an argument. Calling it an argument is because they presented it in the manner of an argument, by way of mockery of them. Or it is from the type of:

*Their greeting among them is a painful blow*

That is, their argument was nothing but what is not an argument. The intended meaning is the negation of their having any argument, for the non-occurrence of a thing now, such as the return of their fathers, which they demanded in this world, does not necessitate its impossibility afterwards, so that the return would be impossible when the Resurrection comes.

The address in (ı'tū, "bring") and (kuntum, "you were") is to the Messenger, upon him be prayer and peace, and the believers, since they are speakers of his statement, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, concerning resurrection, seeking from the disbelievers acknowledgment of it. It is also permitted that it is addressed to him, upon him be prayer and peace, and to the prophets, peace be upon them, who came with the resurrection, and the address has prevailed over the third person.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: (ı'tū, "bring") and (kuntum, "you were") are from the standpoint of addressing him, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and what is meant is he and his Lord, and the angel who is mentioned, upon him be prayer and peace, as having brought this down to him, and he is Gabriel, peace be upon him. And that, as you see, is (questionable).

Al-Hasan, 'Amr ibn 'Ubayd, Ibn 'Amir as narrated from him by 'Abd al-Hamid, 'Asim as narrated by Harun, and Husayn from Abu Bakr from him read (ḥujjatuhum, "their argument") with the nominative (raf'), taking it as the subject (ism) of kāna, and what follows it as the predicate (khabar), meaning: their argument was not anything whatsoever except this false statement. The response (jawāb) of (idhā, "when") is "was not," etc. It is not joined by the fā' (the resumptive "then"), even though it is obligatory in a negated clause when introduced by mā, because (idhā) is neither a jussive particle nor an original conditional particle. This is the secret of the statement of Abu Hayyan: that (idhā), when it differs from the conditional particles, is such that when its response is negated by mā, the fā' is not required, unlike the conditional particles, which require the fā', as in: "If you visit us, then you have not been harsh with us." So there is no need to posit a response for it, such as "they resorted to false arguments," contrary to Ibn Hisham.

It was argued from the occurrence of what has been mentioned as a response that the operation (of the particle) in (idhā) does not belong to the response, because of the prefix mā' which prevents this, and there is no one who makes a distinction. Perhaps whoever says it governs (the preceding word) would say that the adverbial of time is given more latitude than other elements. Then, the meaning is in the future tense due to the position of (idhā), i.e., their argument will not be anything except that they say that.

[Page 155]

Say: "God gives you life" at the beginning, "then He causes you to die" when your appointed terms (ajal) end, as the proofs indicate, not "time" (al-dahr) as you claim. "Then He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection." That is, He will gather you in it. It is permissible that the verb be taken to imply a meaning such as "resurrected" or "brought to an end," but the sense of "in" (fi) is more apparent, meaning that He will gather you on the Day of Resurrection. "There is no doubt about it," that is, about your gathering, for whoever is able to originate is able to restore. Wisdom requires that you be gathered for recompense on that Day without fail. "And the promise is true" is indicated by the verses that strike upon it, that is, that proclaim it. Its summary is that resurrection is a possible matter, reported by the Truthful One and required by wisdom, and whatever is of this kind will certainly come to pass. Bringing back the forefathers (al-ātha' bi'l-ābā') is contrary to legislative wisdom (al-hikma al-tashri'iyya), so its occurrence is impossible. "But most people do not know" is an istidrak (a corrective addition, lit. "catching up") to His saying, "there is no doubt about it." It is either part of the speech that was commanded to be said, or a statement issued from Him, exalted is He, to establish the truth and to alert that their doubt arises from their ignorance and their deficiency in reflection and contemplation, not because there is any trace of doubt in it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 27:

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ This is an explanation of the absolute exclusivity and the all-encompassing control over them, and over what is between them, belonging to Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, following the explanation of His control through giving life, causing death, resurrection, and gathering for recompense. Thus it is a generalization of power after a specification.

﴿And the Day the Hour is established, on that Day the falsifiers will be lost﴾ Al-Zamakhshari said: the operative element in (the Day the Hour is established) is "will be lost," and "on that Day" is a substitute (badal) for "the Day the Hour is established." Ibn 'Atiyya related this from a group of scholars. Placing the adverbial phrase before the verb serves to restrict (the loss to that Day), because every loss at the time of loss on that Day is indeed a loss, and in it there is also observance of the verse-endings (fawasil), as has been said. The substitution view has been challenged on the grounds that the tanwin in ﴿yawma'idhin﴾ is a replacement (iwad) for the sentence it is annexed to, and the apparent meaning is that this sentence is to be supplied by the context of what precedes "the Hour is established." So it is said: "And the Day the Hour is established, the Day when the Hour is established, the falsifiers will be lost," so it becomes an emphatic restatement (ta'kid), not a substitute, since there is no sense in the latter. For this reason it has been said that it more closely resembles emphasis. Abu Hayyan's statement: "If it is a substitute, a confirmative substitute, which is rare, it is permitted; otherwise it is not. It neither fattens nor satisfies" [a proverb meaning it is of no use]. Some have strained and claimed that the second day means a time that is part of the Day of the Hour's establishment, so it is a substitute of a part, with a pronoun-referent understood; and since the manifestation of their loss is in it, it is the intended meaning in relation to it. Another group said: the operative element in (the Day the Hour is established) is what is indicated by the dominion. They said: this is because the Day of Resurrection is a third matter that is neither the heavens nor the earth, since those are transformed; so it is as if it were said: "And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth, and the dominion on the Day the Hour is established." "On that Day" is in the accusative, governed by "will be lost," and the sentence is a resumptive statement (istinaf), even though it has a connection with what precedes it through the tanwin of replacement. It was also said that it may be a conjunction (atf) on an adverbial complement governed by the mentioned "dominion," as if it were said: "To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth today, and on the Day the Hour is established." And this, as you see, is [weak]. "The falsifiers" (al-mubtiluna) are those who enter into falsehood; perhaps what is meant by it is its greatest type, which is disbelief (kufr).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 28:

﴿And you will see every nation﴾ among the nations gathered, ﴿kneeling﴾ (jathiyah), sitting on their knees, alert and tense. This is the posture of the sinner who is fearful and awaits what he dislikes. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that jathiyah means "gathered together." It is related from Qatadah that it means "groups" (jamaʿat), from the root jathwah (with the jim pronounced with three vowels), which is a group that gathers around juthan, i.e., a heap of gathered dust. It is related from Mu'arrij al-Sadusi that jathiyah means "submissive," in the dialect of Quraysh. The address in (tara, "you see") is either to whoever is capable of seeing, or to the master of the addressees, upon him be prayers and peace, and it is visual seeing. (Jathiyah) is a circumstantial accusative (hal), and it has been permitted that it be a qualifier (sifah). If it were a cognitive verb, it would be a second object (maf'ul thani). It has been read as (jadhiyah) with a dhal, and jadhw is more intense in tense posture than juthw, because the jadhi is one who sits on the tips of his toes. It has also been permitted that al-jadhi means al-jathi, with its thaʾ replaced by a dhal, since the thaʾ and dhal are interchangeable, as it is said: shahhath and shahhadh.

﴿Every nation is called to its record﴾, to the book of its deeds which the recording angels wrote, so that it may be reckoned. The singular is used to denote the category; otherwise each individual of each nation has a record in which his deeds are contained. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the book of its prophet, to which it is called so that it may be examined whether it acted upon it or not. This is related from Yahya ibn Salam, except that he took "every nation" to mean every disbelieving nation, while the apparent meaning is generality. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the Preserved Tablet, i.e., it is called to what was decreed for it therein.

Yaʿqub read (kulla) in the accusative, and it has been construed as a substitute (badal) for the first kull. The clause (tud'a, "is called") is a qualifier. The substitution of the nation being called to its record for the kneeling nation is good, and this comes under the category of qualification. The same may be said when the clause is a circumstantial clause. If the seeing is cognitive and the clause ﴿is called﴾ is a second object, then the apparent meaning is that it is an emphasis. Making it an emphasis while the clause is a qualifier involves the insertion of emphasis between the two qualifiers, which, as in al-Kashshaf, is not preferred.

﴿Today you will be recompensed for what you used to do﴾, a quoted speech of a hidden saying, and it is either a circumstantial clause or a predicate after a predicate.

In the speech there is an implied elided noun, i.e., "the recompense of what you used to do," etc., or it is metaphorical.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 29:

His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿This is Our Book﴾ to the end, is part of what is said at that time. The indication (al-ishara) is to the Book to which the nation addressed with this statement is summoned. If it is the Book of Deeds (sahifat al-a'mal), then its attribution to His pronoun, exalted is His majesty, is for the slightest connection, by way of metaphor (tajawwuz) in the relational attribution (al-nisba al-idafiyya), for He, exalted is He, is the One who commanded the scribes (al-kataba) to write their deeds in it. And if the Book is the Book revealed to the Prophet of that nation, or the Preserved Tablet (al-lawh al-mahfuz), then the matter of the attribution is evident. The pronoun of majesty (damir al-azama) in all the other aspects is to magnify the status of the Book. It is also permitted that the pronoun refers to the scribes, and the attribution in it is literal (haqiqiyya). It has been said: "What refutes this is ﴿we were copying﴾, unless it is taken to mean 'we were copying and writing' (nankhu wa-naktub)." And He will know, God willing, what is in it.

In my view, the more apparent reading is to take "the Book" in both places as the Book of Deeds, with the demonstrative (ism al-ishara) as the subject (mubtada') and what follows it as the predicate (khabar). His, glorified is He, saying ﴿speaks against you﴾, i.e., bears witness against you, ﴿with truth﴾ without addition or deficiency, is another predicate, or a circumstantial clause (hal), or a resumed sentence (mustaanaf). "Bi-l-haqq" (with truth) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "yantiq" (speaks). His, may He be exalted, saying ﴿Indeed, We used to copy﴾ to the end is a justification (ta'lil) for its speaking against them about their deeds without omitting anything of them, i.e., "Indeed, We used to copy the angels before this," meaning, We used to make them copy and write ﴿what you used to do﴾ in the world of deeds, whether good or evil. The real meaning of copying (naskh) is writing from an original which is consulted; so it seems that the deeds of the servants are the original, as in al-Bahr (the Sea of Surrounding Waters).

Ibn Jarir reported from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: Indeed God, exalted is He, created the nun, which is the inkwell, and created the pen, and said: "Write." It said: "What shall I write?" He said: "Write what will exist until the Day of Resurrection, of deeds done, righteous or wicked, and provision apportioned, lawful or unlawful." Then He obliged for each of that its clarification: its entry into the world, when; its stay in it, how long; and its exit from it, how. Then He placed over the servants guardians (hafaza), and over the Book treasurers (khazzan). The guardians copy every day from the treasurers the deeds of that day. When the provision is exhausted, the command has ended, and the term has run out, the guardians come to the treasurers seeking the deeds of that day, and the treasurers say: "We find nothing for your companion with us." So they return and find him dead.

Then Ibn 'Abbas said: Are you not a people of Arabic who hear the guardians saying ﴿Indeed, we were copying what you used to do﴾? And is copying (istinsakh) anything but from an original? In a narration of Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim from him, may God be pleased with him, he was asked about the verse, and he mentioned something like what you have heard, then said: "Is anything copied except from a book?" That copying is from the Preserved Tablet has been narrated by a group from him. What we have mentioned indicates that this statement from the angels can be correct without interpreting ﴿nastansikh﴾ as ﴿nansakh﴾, as is not hidden.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 30:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿As for those who believed and did righteous deeds, their Lord will admit them into His mercy﴾ to the end of the verse, is an elaboration (tafsil) of what is implied in the general (mujmal) statement of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿This Book speaks against you with truth﴾, or it is that they are recompensed with the promise and the threat. By "mercy" is meant Paradise, metaphorically, and the particle of place (zarfiyyah) is kept in its apparent sense. It has also been said that by "mercy" is meant what includes Paradise and other than it, but the first (view) is more apparent. ﴿That﴾, which was mentioned, namely being admitted into His mercy, ﴿is the manifest triumph﴾. The apparent meaning is that it is a triumph with no triumph beyond it.

And as for those who disbelieved, [it will be said to them]: "Were My verses not recited to you?" That is, it will be said to them, by way of rebuke and reproach: "Did My messengers not come to you, and were My verses not recited to you?" The answer to "as for" (amma) is the implied statement, and it has been omitted because the intended meaning is clear, namely what is said. Omitting it is very common and follows a recognized pattern, to the point that it has been said, "It is the sea; speak of it." The element coordinated with it has also been omitted, indicated by the conjunctive fa', and the recitation of the verses necessarily implies the coming of the messengers in meaning. This is the view of al-Zamakhshari. The majority hold that the interrogative hamza (alif of interrogation) is placed before the fa' as a result of being moved forward, since interrogatives have precedence, and that the fa' is intended to be understood. The implied sentence is then: "It will be said to them: 'Did they not...'" and there is no omission other than of the verb of saying. In al-Kashshaf, it is said that if it is understood that the omitted element is "so they will be reproached," indicated by what follows it, that is also possible. The benefit of this style, although the original would be "so He will admit them to His punishment," is to indicate that the believers will enter Paradise, while the disbelievers, after them, remain in the place of standing, being punished with reproach. This would be a sound interpretation.

﴿فاسْتَكْبَرْتُمْ﴾ "Then you were arrogant," against believing in them.
﴿وكُنْتُمْ قَوْمًا مُجْرِمِينَ﴾ "And you were a people given to sin," a people whose habit was crime.

﴿وإذا قِيلَ إنَّ وعْدَ اللَّهِ﴾ "And when it was said: 'Indeed the promise of God...'" That is, what He, glorified be He, promised of future matters, or His promise of this, ﴿حَقٌّ﴾ "is true," that is, it is certainly existent, or its object is certainly so. There is therefore a figurative usage in the sentence, either in one of the two terms or in the predication.

And al-A'raj and Amr ibn Qa'id read [it differently].

(And when it was said that) with a fatha on the hamza, according to the dialect of Sulaym, ﴿And the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾, with *al-sā'ah* in the nominative in the reading of the majority, as a conjunction with the position (*maḥall*) of *inna* and its noun, according to what Abu 'Ali (al-Farisi) held and al-Zamakhshari followed. Whoever claimed that the noun of *inna* has a position permitted the conjunction with it here. Abu Hayyan claimed that the correct view is that neither of the two possibilities is permitted. Accordingly, the clause ﴿the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾ is a conjunction with the preceding clause. Hamza read (*wa-al-sā'ata*) with the accusative, as a conjunction with the noun of *inna*. This is also reported from al-A'mash, Abu 'Amr, Abu Haywah, 'Isa, al-'Absi and al-Mufaddal. The mention of the matter of the Hour, and that there is no doubt about its occurrence, although it is among what God the Exalted promised, is an emphasis on the matter of resurrection, which is the aim of the context. ﴿You said﴾, out of extreme obstinacy: ﴿We do not know what the Hour is﴾, that is, what it is, expressing extreme astonishment at it, as the plural form of "we do not know" together with the interrogative indicates.

﴿We only suppose a supposition﴾. This has been found problematic, because it is an exceptive clause with the operator left unexpressed (*mufarragh*), and they have said: it is not permitted to leave the operator unexpressed with a cognate absolute object that is emphatic. So one does not say *mā ḍarabtu illā ḍarban* ("I did not strike except a striking"), because it is equivalent to *mā ḍarabtu illā ḍarabtu* ("I did not strike except I struck"). Al-Radi said: the exceptive clause with the operator left unexpressed must be an exception from an assumed plural that is inflected according to the case of the excepted item, comprising the entire genus, so that the excepted item enters it with certainty and then is excluded by the exception. The verbal noun of *naẓunnu* is not something that admits, alongside supposition, anything else from which supposition would be excluded. The same is said of *mā ḍarabtu illā ḍarban* and similar constructions. This is what is meant by those who said it is of the type of excepting a thing from itself. They differed in its resolution. It was said: the meaning of *mā naẓunnu* is "we do not perform supposition," as in *qīma* and *quʿida* (impersonal passives), and then the exception is valid, the locus of negation and affirmation differs in terms of the assumed and the figurative in the exception from the general assumed. Making *naẓunnu* mean "we do not perform the act" rather than "we do not perform supposition" is as if it were said: "we do not perform any act except supposition." The same applies to its like. Among such examples is the verse of al-A'sha:

*And grey hair alighted upon him with its burdens, and grey hair deceived him only with deception.*

Sahib al-Kashf approved this. It was also said: *mā naẓunnu* is by way of *mā naʿtaqidu* ("we do not believe"), and *ẓannan* is the object, meaning: "we do not believe anything except supposition." Abu Hayyan approved this. It was objected that the apparent state of them is that they are wavering, not believing. It was answered that the negated belief does not contradict their apparent state but rather confirms it in the most complete manner. It was also said: the excepted item is the supposition of the matter of the Hour, and the excepted-from is supposition in general, as if it were said: "there is no supposition and no hesitation for us except supposition of the matter of the Hour, and hesitation about it." So the speech is for negating their supposition regarding anything else, as an intensification. Al-Radi said: *mā ḍarabtu illā ḍarban* allows multiplicity from the standpoint of the addressee's supposition, for you may say "I struck," while he supposes you did something other than striking, such as its preliminaries, like threatening; so you repel that and say "I struck a striking." It is like *jāʾa Zaydun Zaydun* ("Zayd came, Zayd"). Since *ḍarabtu* admits striking and other things by way of supposition, it becomes like the multiple that includes striking and other things. Its gist is that since striking, before emphasis and exception, admitted another act, it was taken in a general sense by the indication of the exception, so the meaning is "I did nothing except striking." Likewise ﴿We only suppose a supposition﴾, and this is nearly identical with what we mentioned first. It was refuted: the exception requires the actual inclusiveness, and a merely supposed possibility does not suffice for it, let alone an imagined one.

It was objected that this is nothing, for when the verb is stripped to a general meaning, the inclusiveness becomes actual. Moreover, the insufficiency of a hypothetical inclusiveness is not granted, as one who examines its instances will know. Ibn Ya'ish and Abu al-Baqa' held that it is by inversion, anteriority and posteriority, and the original is *in naḥnu illā naẓunnu ẓannan* ("we are only supposing a supposition"). This is reported from al-Mubarrad, and what Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' and Sibawayh recorded from the Arabs' saying *laysa al-ṭību illā al-misku* (with *al-misk* in the nominative) has been taken as an instance of it. He said: the original is *laysa illā al-ṭība al-misku*, so that the noun of *laysa* is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*), and what follows *illā*, subject and predicate, is in the place of the predicate of *laysa*. Al-Radi rejected this, saying it is far-fetched because of the complication it contains, which spoils eloquence.

The example reported is in the dialect of Banu Tamim, for they treated *laysa* like *mā* and left it inoperative, because the negation is annulled by *illā*. It was also said that *ẓannan* is an absolute object of an omitted verb, and the excepted item is omitted, and the estimate is: "we only suppose, except that you suppose a supposition."

It is also reported from al-Mubarrad, and in it is the omission of *inna*, its noun and its predicate, with retention of the verbal noun, which is not permitted. In it too is the complication that spoils eloquence to the extent it does. I do not think the report of it from al-Mubarrad is correct, given its extreme coldness. The author of al-Taqrib permitted that the meaning is "we only suppose a supposition, a weak one," so it is an explanatory verbal noun of the kind, its attribute omitted, as al-Bahr explicitly states, and not an emphatic one. This agrees with what Imam al-Sakkaki mentioned in one discussion, that indefiniteness may be for belittlement. It was objected that the saying of God the Exalted ﴿and we are not certain﴾ rules this out, for the opposite of certainty is supposition in general, not its weak kind. Several have stated that this clause is like an emphasis of what precedes it, and its intent is the continuation and emphasis of the negation. It was said: the meaning is "we are not certain of the possibility of the Hour," that is, we are not certain of its possibility at all, let alone of its actual occurrence, which is indicated by His saying ﴿Indeed the promise of God is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt about it﴾. Their saying this is a rejection of that. Perhaps those who attributed to themselves supposition without certainty regarding the matter of the Hour are not those who said ﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, for that is evident that they deny resurrection and are firmly certain of the negation of the Hour. So the unbelievers are of two kinds: one kind is firm in negating it, like their leaders, and another kind is wavering and perplexed about it. When they hear what is transmitted from their forefathers, they deny it, and when they hear the recited verses, their denial recedes and they waver.

It is possible that the speaker of the one and the speaker of the other is the same, but each saying belongs to a time and state, and whoever is in a state of fluctuation with varying states: at times he is firm in negation and says ﴿There is only our life of this world﴾, and at other times he supposes and says ﴿We only suppose a supposition﴾. It was said: firmness there is in negating its occurrence, and supposition without certainty here is merely regarding its possibility. So they are wavering about its intrinsic possibility, yet firm in its non-occurrence in fact. So reflect.

(The twenty-fifth part is complete, and next, God willing, is the twenty-sixth part, whose beginning is ﴿And there will appear to them﴾.)

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿And there appeared to them﴾, that is, became manifest to them at that time, ﴿the evils of what they had done﴾, that is, the ugly consequences of their deeds, meaning their punishments, for punishment harms its recipient and appears ugly to him. Or it means the evil deeds of them, that is, their evil actions, with the annexation (idafa) being of a descriptive adjective to the thing described, and the statement being according to an elided noun, meaning: there appeared to them the recompense of that. Or the evils may mean their recompense, by way of naming the cause for the effect.

It has also been said: the intended meaning is that there appeared to them the evil aspects of their actions, which are not good according to reason, that is, the aspects of their rational ugliness (qubḥ al-ʿaqlī) which were hidden from them in the world by Satan's embellishment. This is a statement affirming the rational good (ḥusn) and rational evil (qubḥ) in actions. Here "mā" is a relative pronoun, and it has been permitted that it be a verbal-masdar particle (maṣdariyya), so it is not to be overlooked.

﴿And there befell them﴾, that is, there descended upon them, ﴿what they used to mock at﴾, namely the recompense and the punishment.

Then it will be said: "Today We shall forsake you, just as you forsook the meeting of this your Day." (Ruh al-Ma'ani, on 45:34)

﴿وقِيلَ اليَوْمَ نَنْساكُمْ﴾ "We shall forsake you," meaning We shall leave you in punishment. This is by way of naming the cause for the effect (min bab iṭlāq al-sabab ʿalā al-musabbab), since whoever forgets something leaves it; or it means We shall make you like a forgotten thing, disregarded and of no account. On this reading there is a figurative metaphor in the form of a depiction (istiʿārah tamthīliyyah). It is also permitted that it be a implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah) in the pronoun of address.

﴿كَما نَسِيتُمْ﴾ "just as you forsook" in the world, ﴿لِقاءَ يَوْمِكم هَذا﴾ "the meeting of this your Day." That is: just as you abandoned its provision, which is piety (taqwā) and faith in it; or just as you did not care about meeting it and did not let it come to mind, like a thing that is cast aside and forgotten. It is also permitted that the expression of "forgetting" it refers to the fact that its knowledge is fixed in their innate nature (fiṭrah), or to their being able to perceive it through the manifest signs of it; thus in the first "forgetting" there is a mushākalah (correspondence of wording). The idafah (construct) of "liqāʾ" to "yawm" is an idafah of the verbal noun to its time-frame, so it carries the sense of "in" (fī), and the object is implied: that is, your meeting with God Most High and His recompense, glorified is He, on this your Day.

Al-ʿAllāmah al-Taftazānī said: "Liqāʾ yawmikum" is like "makr al-layl" (the cunning of the night), of the type of metaphor in predication (al-majāz al-ḥukmī); therefore the annexed noun is treated as the object. It was not made an idafah of the verbal noun to its direct object in the literal sense, because the rebuke is not over forgetting the meeting with the Day itself, but over forgetting what is in it of recompense.

Some of the eminent scholars said: It is not hidden that "liqāʾ al-yawm" may be a kinayah (metonymy) for meeting all that is in it, and this is more fitting to the context, since the context is about denying the resurrection.

﴿ومَأْواكُمُ النّارُ وما لَكم مِن ناصِرِينَ﴾ "Your refuge is the Fire, and you have no helpers" meaning: none of you has a single helper who will rescue you from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 35:

﴿That﴾ (the punishment) ﴿is because you﴾, that is, because of the fact that ﴿you took the signs of Allah in mockery﴾, meaning as things to be mocked, and you did not lift your heads to them. ﴿The worldly life deceived you﴾, so you reckoned that there was no life other than it. ﴿So today they will not be brought out of it﴾, that is, out of the Fire.

al-Hasan, Ibn Thabbat, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read (lā yakhrujūn) in the active voice. The shift to the third person (al-iltifat ila al-ghaybah) serves to indicate that they have been removed from the rank of direct address, as a way of showing contempt for them, or that they have been moved from the station of being addressed to the depths of the Fire (ghaybat al-nar). It is also permissible that this be the beginning of a new statement, in which case there is no shift (iltifat).

﴿Nor will they be asked to make amends﴾, that is, it will not be demanded of them that they appease their Lord, glory be to Him, that is, that they remove His displeasure, exalted is He. This is a metaphor (kinayah) for seeking His pleasure, meaning that it will not be demanded of them that they win His approval, mighty and majestic is He, because the time for it has passed. This was discussed earlier in (Surat) al-Rum and al-Sajdah, and there are other interpretations of it there, so refer back to them.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 36:

﴿So all praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the heavens and Lord of the earth, Lord of the worlds.﴾ This is a consequence (tafri') of what the noble surah contains. It contains the favors (ala') and bounties (afdal) of Allah, the Exalted, the Majestic, and it includes the signs (dala'il) of the horizons and of the self, and it encompasses (intawat) the clear proofs and the shining texts concerning the beginning (mabda') and the return (ma'ad). The lam here denotes exclusive ownership (likhtisas), the fronting of the predicate (taqdim al-khabar) serves to emphasize it, and the definiteness of "al-hamd" (praise) is for comprehensiveness (istighraq) or for the genus (jins). The sentence is an informative statement (ikhbar) about His deserving praise because of what it indicates, though it is also permitted that it be understood as a performative statement (insha'). The full discussion of this has already been given in al-Fatiha. As for the consequence mentioned, it is, according to what some eminent scholars (ajilla) have said, an indication that their disbelief does not affect His lordship in any way, and does not block the path of His beneficence and mercy, the Majestic, the Exalted, just as the abundant rain cloud is not blocked. Rather, they have only wronged themselves. The attributes that are mentioned, indicating His bounty upon them, function as evidence for His deserving praise and for His being exclusively worthy of it, the Exalted, the Most High. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Lord of the worlds﴾, is a substitute (badal) for what precedes it. The repetition of the word "Lord" carries emphasis and signals that His lordship over everything is by way of essential ownership (asala). Ibn Muhaysin read it with a nominative ending (raf'), as an expression of praise (madh), with an implied pronoun, which is ho

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 45, verse 37:

﴿And His is the greatness﴾ carries the same exclusivity as ﴿So to Allah belongs all praise﴾. Ibn al-Athir said that al-kibriya' (greatness) means magnificence and sovereignty. Al-Raghib (al-Isfahani) said that it means rising above submission to others. It has also been said that it is an expression for the perfection of the Essence and the perfection of Existence. The phrase ﴿in the heavens and the earth﴾ is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) or is connected to ﴿greatness﴾. Restricting it in this way is because the effects and rulings of greatness are manifest in them. The use of the explicit noun in place of a pronoun is to glorify the status of greatness. In the sacred hadith (hadith qudsi, a saying of the Prophet in which Allah speaks in the first person): "Greatness is My cloak and majesty is My waist-wrapper; whoever disputes with Me over either of them, I will cast into the Fire." It was narrated by Imam Ahmad, Muslim, Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wal-Sifat (The Divine Names and Attributes), from Abu Hurayrah. This clearly indicates that greatness and majesty are not identical, so do not overlook this. ﴿And He is the Mighty﴾, whom none can overcome, ﴿the Wise﴾ in everything He decrees and ordains. In these clauses there is guidance, as has been said, to noble commands, as if it were said: To Him belongs praise, so praise Him, the Exalted; to Him belongs greatness, so declare His greatness, glorified is He; and He is the Mighty, the Wise, so obey Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Some scholars took these to be a metaphor or an allusion to the commands mentioned. And Allah knows best. Furthermore, from the perspective of isharah (esoteric allusion), I have not found anything relating to any of the verses of this noble surah that is worth the effort of transmitting, other than what relates to His saying: ﴿And He has subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, all of it from Him﴾, namely interpreting it as an allusion to wahdat al-wujud (the unity of existence). This has already been mentioned, which makes repeating it unnecessary. And Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, is the Granter of success.
